---
title: "Point-by-Point Response to Reviewers"
subtitle: "MSB-2026-13900 — Resolving cell-cell communication programs beyond cell-type boundaries across conditions"
---

We thank both reviewers for their very thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our manuscript.
These points have been extremely helpful in improving our manuscript.
Below, we include each reviewer comment followed by our point-by-point response.

## Reviewer #1

> The authors present CCC-RISE, an extension of their PARAFAC2-based RISE framework to cell-cell communication (CCC).
> Rather than pseudobulking single-cell data into fixed cell-type labels, CCC-RISE computes ligand-receptor (LR) communication scores between label-free "eigen-states," assembles a 4-D tensor (sender eigen-state x receiver eigen-state x LR pair x condition), factorizes it by canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD), and projects the resulting components back onto individual cells.
> The stated advance is a method that models communication across conditions while retaining single-cell resolution, thereby exposing signaling subpopulations that cut across conventional cell-type boundaries.
> The method is applied to a COVID-19 bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cohort and a lung-transplant (ALAD) cohort.
>
> The method is conceptually well-motivated, the manuscript is clearly written, and the eigen-state -> CPD -> cell-mapping construction is elegant and addresses a genuine limitation of existing tensor-based CCC tools.
> However, in its current form the central claims are inadequately validated: the only quantitative benchmark is constructed in a biased manner, the "resolution" claim is not quantified, and there is an unaddressed methodological concern in the communication score itself.

We appreciate the reviewer's assessment that the eigen-state → CPD → cell-mapping construction is elegant and addresses a genuine limitation.
We agree that our approach to validation was limited both in its approach, and in a disconnect between what should have been the goal (validating the communication scoring itself), and implementation (assessing the strength of association with clinical features).

Following the reviewers' suggestions, we have comprehensively re-worked our approach to validation of the model, and added a variety of quantitative validation metrics to evaluate the communication scoring itself.
In the process, we think that this validation work also serves to better explain the construction of our approach.
Also, as detailed below, we now compare our results to a broad panel of existing approaches, and use these comparisons to demonstrate the relative strengths of our approach.

### Major concerns

> 1. No comparison to any published method.
>    The introduction correctly places the work against a broad landscape of tools, but none of them are actually run.
>    The sole benchmark (Fig. 2e-h) is against a "pseudobulk CPD equivalent" that the authors build themselves by averaging within cell types before applying the same pipeline.
>    Because that baseline discards subpopulation structure by construction, the demonstration that CCC-RISE recovers subpopulation structure is close to self-fulfilling.
>    The paper needs quantitative comparison against real tools in terms of AUC/accuracy:
>    - For the single-cell-resolution claim: Scriabin (Wilk et al., Nat Biotech 2023), and ideally NICHES/DeepCOLOR, which are already cited but not run.
>      Here, you could use a multi-condition dataset analyzed condition-by-condition with Scriabin, then compare to CCC-RISE's per-cell loadings; this would demonstrate that there is actual value in the multi-condition modelling.
>      In addition, how does CCC-RISE perform on a single-condition task/dataset?
>      Does its performance degrade compared to Scriabin?
>    - For the multi-condition tensor claim: Tensor-cell2cell (Armingol et al., the actual tool) and/or STACCato, which are the closest methodological competitors.
>      For this, please also report ALAD status AUC as for CCC-RISE

[Needs to be updated based on final comparator work.]
Points to address are:
- single-cell resolution validation (concordance with NICHES, problems with Scriabin),
- single-condition performance (problems with Scriabin),
- and multi-condition tensor validation (similarities/differences with Tensor-cell2cell, STACCato, and pseudobulk)

We agree that a self-constructed pseudobulk baseline cannot carry this claim, and we now benchmark against the published methods the reviewer names.
To run them on equal footing, we re-implemented Scriabin, NICHES, and STACCato in Python from the upstream algorithms, and we drive all of themfrom the same ligand-receptor resource and normalized expression, so each comparison isolates the contribution of the algorithm (l. XXX).

For the single-cell-resolution claim, we reconstruct a per-cell-pair communication score from CCC-RISE (per-cell RISE projections combined with the sender, receiver, and LR pair CPD factors) and compare it against Scriabin's and NICHES' per-cell-pair edge weights on the same sampled sender/receiver cells and the same LR pairs, reporting rank concordance per condition (Fig. XXX).
We repeat this on a single-condition subset to test directly whether CCC-RISE degrades relative to Scriabin when there is no cross-condition structure to exploit, and report where the multi-condition model does and does not add value (l. XXX).
We anticipate that CCC-RISE is strongly concordant with Scriabin within a condition --- the two agree on which cell pairs signal --- while the multi-condition model is what makes the resulting programs comparable *across* conditions, which is the claim the manuscript actually rests on.

For the multi-condition tensor claim, we run Tensor-cell2cell and STACCato on a communication tensor built from the same data and report ALAD-status classification performance (AUC, under the same cross-validation scheme) for all three methods side by side (Fig. XXX, l. XXX).

We did not run DeepCOLOR: its distinguishing contribution over Scriabin and NICHES is spatial-colocalization inference, and neither cohort has matched spatial data, so it would be run outside the regime for which it was designed.
We discuss this in the revised text (l. XXX).

> 2. The central claim is not quantitatively supported.
>    The claims "superior granularity" and "subpopulations invisible to aggregate methods" are supported only by qualitative PaCMAP embeddings and communication-score heatmaps.
>    There is no ground-truth evaluation and no metric establishing that CCC-RISE recovers real structure that existing baselines miss.
>    I recognize the field lacks gold standards, but simulation frameworks with defined communication ground truth exist (e.g., the SERGIO-based CCC simulator) and would allow the authors to quantify the resolution advantage.
>    At minimum, the manuscript should provide a quantitative concordance/discordance analysis against Scriabin on the same data.

[Also needs to be updated once comparator work is complete.]

We agree that our qualitative observations did not adequatley support this claim.
Our revision adds three quantitative lines of reasoning/evidence.

First, we over-hauled our strategy for defining subpopulations beyond classical cell-type boundaries.
The reviewer is correct to point out the weakness of the qualitative PaCMAP embeddings and communication-score heatmaps.
Instead, we now define subpopulations based on quantitative per-cell sender and receiver loadings derived from the projection matrices and sender/receiver factor matrices.
For more detail on our new strategy, we point the reviewer to {{< panel 2 sender-receiver-strata >}}, {{< panel 4 hormone-angle-scatter >}}, and Methods section [XXX].

[Update based on NicheNet comparator results. Otherwise, done.]
Second, as a real-data accuracy metric, we tested each component against an independent, literature-curated ligand to downstream-target prior (the NicheNet v2 ligand--target matrix)\ [@doi:10.1038/s41592-019-0667-5; @doi:10.1038/s41596-024-01121-9].
Briefly, for each component, we compare the differentially expressed genes in top receiver cells with each ligand's NicheNet target genes to derive a NicheNet score per ligand, then we take a weighted average of ligand scores weighted by each ligand's loading to determine if top-weighted ligands' target genes are over-expressed in receiver cells.
We apply this pipeline to CCC-RISE and to each comparator method.
For more detail on this extension of the NicheNet database, we point the reviewer to
{{< panel 2 nichenet >}}, [Figure 5 NicheNet reference], and Methods section [XXX].
One limitation that we encountered in this analysis is that there is only moderate overlap between the LR pairs highlighted by our method, and the NicheNet target database, due to the limited coverage of the latter.

[Update with Scriabin result]
Third, as a quantitative evaluation of sender and receiver cell loadings, we report a concordance analysis against NICHES, which we discussed extensively above in response to Reviewer #1 Comment #1.
As explained there, while we would have liked to report concordance with Scriabin, ...

We deliberately did not build the suggested analysis on a SERGIO-style simulator.
Simulated communication ground truth is generated under an assumed model of how ligand--receptor signaling shapes expression, and agreement with it mainly certifies that our score matches that assumption; where a simulation disagrees with the real-data result, it is not clear which should be believed.
We judged that, while the field suffers from well-defined gold standards, many of the other suggestions from the reviewers here provide stronger evidence of CCC-RISE working on real data (l. XXX).

> 3. Sign ambiguity in the communication score.
>    The communication score is the outer product of a sender eigen-state's ligand loading and a receiver eigen-state's receptor loading (if I am not mistaken).
>    PARAFAC2/RISE factors are not constrained to be non-negative (initialization is by SVD and it is run on mean centered data), so eigenstate gene loadings can be negative.
>    A negative ligand loading multiplied by a negative receptor loading results in a spurious positive communication score, and the biological meaning of "negative ligand expression of an eigenstate" is unclear.
>    The authors should state explicitly how signs are handled before and after the outer product, and demonstrate that the reported components are not driven by sign artifacts.
>    This is fundamental, since the entire tensor is built from this score.

The reviewer is correct, and investigating this issue helped us to clarify what the factor loadings of CCC-RISE represent.
Eigen-state gene loadings are estimated relative to a single, fixed per-gene mean computed once over the full dataset before RISE is fit; the loading itself is therefore a *deviation* from that mean, not an expression level, and can legitimately be negative.
The outer product previously used for scoring, however, was taken directly on these signed deviations.
Writing actual expression as (mean + deviation) for both partners shows why this is a problem: the full product expands to $\mu_L\mu_R + \mu_L\Delta_R + \mu_R\Delta_L + \Delta_L\Delta_R$, and the prior score kept only the last term, $\Delta_L\Delta_R$---the interaction term, with baseline and main effects discarded.
That term alone has no reliable relationship to actual signaling strength, which is exactly why two negative deviations produced a spurious positive score indistinguishable from two positive ones.

We have changed the communication score to add the per-gene mean back to each eigen-state's ligand/receptor loading before scoring, so that the score is computed on an approximation of actual non-negative expression rather than on centered loadings directly.
This uses the same centering reference as RISE and makes every entry of the communication tensor non-negative by construction, which we then verified empirically holds across both datasets.
We describe this convention explicitly in the Methods section [XXX].

[Revisit proposed discussion point (last sentence)]
We also considered decomposing each eigen-state into separate non-negative positive- and negative-loading components (analogous to how non-negative matrix factorization resolves a signed PCA-like axis into two unipolar programs).
We have independent evidence, from a companion investigation that compares PARAFAC2 to other methods such as iNMF, MOFA+, etc., that this bidirectional structure often represents coherent biology rather than noise.
For instance, ablating the minority-sign arm of a component measurably degrades held-out reconstruction, and non-negative methods independently recover the same positive/negative split as two distinct, functionally coherent, antagonistic programs.
We ultimately did not adopt this as the primary fix because it doubles the sender/receiver dimension of the communication tensor and still requires classifying which cells belong to which arm, whereas re-centering the score resolves the non-negativity concern directly without changing the rank of the model.
We note the bidirectional-loading evidence in the Discussion as a data point for why we did not additionally constrain RISE itself to be non-negative (see response to Reviewer #2, minor comment #3).

[ACTUALLY, I wonder if this paragraph can be dropped. It goes beyond the reviewer's concerns.]
[Revisit proposed result point (last sentence). There is an example of flipped signs in an IBD component but we do not explicitly talk about it. Could discuss that component exclusively here.]
Finally, we also evaluated whether the communication tensor should be factored with the factor matrices constrained to be non-negative.
Across multiple datasets, we observed that this constraint significantly reduced the ability of factorization to impute held-out data, indicating that it reduced the fidelity of the factorization as a representation of the communication scoring.
Therefore, we retained the communication tensor factorization as signed, and use our results as an opportunity to explain how these signs should be interpreted (l. XXX)

> 4. Risk of overfitting in the ALAD classifier.
>    For the ALAD cohort, the number of eigenstates and CPD components were selected because they "yielded the optimal predictive performance for ALAD status".
>    The Methods do describe repeated, stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 5 repeats; however, the rank selection (number of eigen-states and CPD components) appears to be performed on the full dataset against the same predictive objective, outside those folds?
>    Unless rank selection is performed inside the cross-validation folds (nested CV), the reported AUC is optimistically biased.
>    Please clarify the CV scheme and, if selection was not nested, re-estimate performance with nested CV.

We have substantially revised our approach to rank selection to address the overfitting concern and to improve the interpretability of the results.
Briefly, we now use a bi-cross-validation (BiCV) scheme to select RISE rank and a cross-component collinearity and stability analysis to select CPD rank, none of which see the sample labels.
In addition to providing a benchmark for the rank selection, the internal BiCV scheme also provides a more reliable estimate of the classifier's performance as it is exposed only to the molecular data and not to the sample labels.
Further, selecting the decomposition rank based on an external prediction limited the use of our approach to applications where such a prediction was available, which the new rank selection scheme avoids.
Our response to Reviewer #2 Comment #4 discusses the new rank selection procedure in depth and Reviewer #1 Comment #5 expands upon the limitations of our previous approach.
The new rank selection results are showcased in [Figure 2a--d] and [Figure S_ibd_rank_selection] and the procedure is described in Methods section [XXX].

> 5. Small samples and no independent validation of the classifier.
>    The COVID cohort has 12 samples; fitting an 18-component L1 logistic regression at the patient level is prone to overfitting.
>    There is no external cohort reproducing the classifier.
>    The authors' own finding that the components do not predict CLAD or death should be stated more prominently, as it shows limitations of the clinical claims.

We agree on both counts.
The twelve-sample COVID-19 cohort has been replaced as the primary demonstration by the ALAD dataset, and we supplement this with the IBDverse terminal-ileum biopsy cohort (343 samples; 232 healthy and 111 Crohn's disease), which is large enough to support patient-level association testing.

We have also changed how condition associations are tested.
In data not shown here, L1-penalized logistic regression proved unstable in exactly the way this comment anticipates: with collinear components, the penalty selects arbitrarily among them, and the selected regularization strength varies from resample to resample, so the identity of the "predictive" components changed with rank and with the bootstrap draw.
We therefore opted to test component--condition associations by ANOVA, applied identically to both datasets, with multiple-testing correction across components and outcomes.
We describe the new association testing in [Figure 3A, S_alad_associations], [Figure 4XXX], and Methods section [XXX]

[Need to confirm these claims are present in text]
On the negative result: with the rank-selection overhaul and new association testing methodology, this result has flipped.
Now, in the ALAD cohort, a single component shows a graded, statistically significant association with six-month outcome after correction, and the same component is significantly associated with six-month and one-year death, as shown in [Fig3A] and [S_alad_associations].
Instead, we fail to identify any communication programs associated with ALAD status, which is now stated in the Results rather than left to the reader to notice [Results XXX].
We discuss why: with 47 samples from 45 recipients and few events, the cohort has limited statistical power, and the significant associations depend on a small number of highly weighted samples [Discussion XXX]
We accordingly frame the clinical claims as hypothesis-generating [Discussion XXX].

> 6. No significance testing for communication programs.
>    Unlike CellPhoneDB/CellChat, CCC-RISE provides no null model or significance assessment for whether a component's communication exceeds chance.
>    The components are interpreted as biologically real throughout without statistical or systematic biological validation; a permutation-based or otherwise principled null would substantially strengthen these interpretations.

We agree and have implemented two complementary permutation-based null models for the communication tensor covering both kinds of significance questions CellPhoneDB/CellChat and dedicated differential-CCC tools such as scDiffCom together provide.

The first asks whether a given tensor entry is unusual at all, the direct analogue of CellPhoneDB/CellChat's own null, which permutes discrete cell-cluster labels and recomputes each cluster pair's mean-expression score.
RISE has no discrete clusters and so we generalize the permutation accordingly: within each condition, we shuffle the cell's raw expression each eigen-state loading row is paired with, and recompute the communication tensor from these shuffled pairings.
This breaks the real cell/eigen-state association while holding cell counts, the loading distribution, and LR identity fixed, giving every tensor entry an empirical p-value (and a z-score, from the same null's mean and standard deviation) against a null of "random" eigen-state assignment.
The results of this permutation test are contained within [Figure 2 significance] and the approach is defined in Methods section [XXX].

A second test answers whether an entry differs between two groups of samples, akin to scDiffCom's own permutation scheme.
We adapted this to CCC-RISE's structure directly: since the communication tensor already has one slice per sample along its condition axis (the same axis as the CPD condition factor), we permute *which existing sample-slice counts as which group*, rather than resampling cells and rebuilding the tensor, allowing us to calculate this test exactly and efficiently.
We report the results of this permutation test within [Figure 3 significance] and the approach is defined in Methods section [XXX].

> 7. Missing multi-condition/differential CCC baselines from the literature.
>    Several directly relevant multi-condition CCC methods are absent from the reference list entirely and should be discussed:
>
>    - scDiffCom (Lagger et al., Nat Aging 2023), a dedicated differential CCC between conditions with permutation-based significance (c.f. comment #6).
>    - CrossTalkeR (Nagai et al., Bioinformatics 2021), differential LR-network analysis across conditions.

We have added both methods as well as NATMI to the Introduction and the reference list\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x; @doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btab370; @doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z].
These methods collectively define an additional class of CCC-inference approaches that analyze conditions in a pair-wise manner, and they are introduced accordingly.

> 8. Inconsistency between the "label-free" premise and label-dependent interpretation.
>    Every program is ultimately described through annotated cell types, and annotations are explicitly reused.
>    The framing that CCC-RISE works "beyond cell-type boundaries" should either be tones down or it should be demonstrated for least one program how biological identity was established without using pre-existing labels.

This is a good point.
We have revised the manuscript to consistently work directly with the cell eigen-states, and explicitly call out where these do or do not align with independent cell-type annotations.

As a concrete demonstration, the ALAD component 5 describing BTC--EGFR signaling is defined entirely from eigen-state loadings: classifying every cell by its sender and receiver loading percentiles, without reference to any annotation, separates a population that is a strong receiver but not a strong sender for this program and vice versa [Figure 2 XXX].
Only afterward do we ask what the existing annotations call these cells, and the answer is the point: the sender and receiver groups are distinct subpopulations of epithelial cells.
Annotations are thus used as an interpretive check on label-free structure rather than as its input, and we have rewritten the relevant passages to make that order explicit rather than describing every program through its cell-type labels [Figure 2 groupings], [Figure 3 groupings], and [Figure 4 groupings].

## Reviewer #2

> This manuscript presents CCC-RISE, a computational framework for inferring cell-cell communication (CCC) programs across multiple biological conditions while preserving single-cell resolution.
> The method extends the RISE framework (based on PARAFAC2) to project cells from multi-condition scRNA-seq data onto shared latent eigen-states-continuous transcriptional programs that capture cellular heterogeneity without requiring predefined cell-type labels.
> Communication scores are computed between eigen-states for all ligand-receptor pairs across conditions, forming a 4D tensor that is decomposed via Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) into interpretable communication programs defined by sender states, receiver states, LR pairs, and conditions.
> The framework is applied to COVID-19 severity and lung transplant (ALAD) cohorts, identifying disease-associated communication programs and tracing them to specific signaling subpopulations.
>
> The conceptual integration of PARAFAC2-based dimensionality reduction with tensor decomposition for CCC analysis is innovative and addresses a current limitation.
> However, in its current form, the manuscript does not establish CCC-RISE as a practical tool.
> Several methodological justifications and validation gaps should be well addressed.
> The methodological descriptions are also confusing, with inconsistent mathematical symbols.

We thank the reviewer for recognizing the conceptual contribution, and we agree that the original submission did not establish CCC-RISE as a practical tool.
The revision addresses this on three fronts: quantitative evaluation against published methods and against a curated ligand-to-target prior (Comments #1 and #2); a principled, dataset-agnostic procedure for choosing both ranks, together with a stability analysis across subsampling and random seeds (Comment #4); and a rewritten Methods section that follows the Fig. 1 pipeline order with a single consistent set of symbols (Comment #6).
We have additionally replaced the twelve-sample COVID-19 cohort with the 343-sample IBDverse cohort, corrected the communication score so that it operates on non-negative expression (Comment #3), and added permutation-based significance testing.
Point-by-point responses follow.

### Major Comments

> 1. The authors demonstrate CCC-RISE's performance through specific examples but do not provide any quantitative evaluation of its accuracy (e.g., precision, recall).
>    It is important to show how well the method recovers known communication patterns and how it performs relative to established approaches.
>    The authors should include simulated data experiments with known ground-truth CCC to evaluate CCC-RISE's accuracy and systematically compare against existing methods (e.g., Tensor-cell2cell) and the reported pseudobulk method in this study, using both simulated and real datasets.
>    Can CCC-RISE recover all communication patterns revealed by these traditional cell-type-based tensor decomposition methods?
>    The current comparison analysis shows that the inferred communication patterns by CCC-RISE are very different from those of the pseudobulk method (Fig. 2b vs. Fig. S1i), except for the two components highlighted by the authors.
>    One notable difference is the learned condition factor matrix.
>    These results suggest that CCC-RISE may miss many meaningful communication patterns revealed by the cell-type-based methods.

[Need to review comparator paragraphs after comparator work is finalized.]
<!-- - Quantitative metrics for recovery of "real" biology (NicheNet, NICHES, reference R1 C1 for NICHES, R1 C2 for NicheNet)
<!-- - Performance relative to comparators (tensor-based methods, reference R1 C1)
<!-- - Refusal to use synthetic data (should re-state for this reviewer or reference R1 C2)-->

We agree, and we have added quantitative evaluation and communication program recovery between methods; much of this overlaps with Reviewer #1 Comments #1 and #2, which we summarize here.

We take two approaches to quantify recovery of "real" biology.
First, we compare differentially expressed genes in each component's receiver cells with each ligand's downstream gene targets, as defined by the NicheNet v2 ligand--target matrix\ [@doi:10.1038/s41592-019-0667-5; @doi:10.1038/s41596-024-01121-9].
This analysis is discussed in detail in Reviewer #1 Comment #2, {{< panel 2 nichenet >}}, and Methods section [XXX].
Second, we measure the concordance between cells with high CCC-RISE sender/receiver weights and cells classified as senders/receivers by NICHES\ [source].
This analysis is discussed in detail in Reviewer #1 Comment #1, [Figure XXX], and Methods section [XXX].

[Update based on comparator results, reference R1 C1]
Additionally, we now run Tensor-cell2cell and STACCato (the closest multi-condition tensor methods) and Scriabin and NICHES (the closest single-cell-resolution methods) on the same data, from the same LR resource and preprocessing, and report head-to-head performance: condition-status classification AUC for the tensor methods and per-cell-pair score concordance for the single-cell methods (Fig. XXX, l. XXX).
[Consolidate into R1 C2 and reference]
Because no cohort carries experimentally established communication ground truth, our accuracy metric is recovery of curated ligand → downstream-target relationships (NicheNet ligand-activity AUROC) in the receiver cells each component implicates --- reported for CCC-RISE, for the pseudobulk equivalent, and for the comparator methods where their output permits it (Fig. XXX).

[Update based on comparator results, reference R1 C1, or cut]
On whether CCC-RISE recovers what cell-type-based decomposition finds: we now report an explicit matched-component comparison against the pseudobulk CPD model, giving for each pseudobulk component its best-matching CCC-RISE component and the congruence of that match per mode (Fig. XXX).
We would also note that the two models are not estimating the same quantity, and we have made this clearer in the text (l. XXX).
The pseudobulk tensor is built from cell-type means, so its components describe communication between cell types; CCC-RISE describes the *variation* in communication across conditions at eigen-state resolution, where a single cell-type-level pattern may be split across eigen-states that cut within a type, and a program confined to a subpopulation is diluted --- and may be absent --- in the cell-type average.
A component-for-component correspondence is therefore not the expected result, and where it fails we now say which of the two behaviors is responsible instead of presenting the discrepancy without comment.
The condition-factor differences the reviewer notes are largely a consequence of this: both the rank and the condition-association test have changed in the revision (see comment #4 and comment #5), and the revised comparison is made at the ranks each model's own selection criterion supports.

We chose these quantitations over a simulated ground truth (e.g. SERGIO-based CCC simulators) because a simulator encodes an assumed model of how signaling shapes expression; recovering it certifies agreement with that assumption rather than with the biology of these tissues.
We state this reasoning in the manuscript rather than leaving the omission unexplained [Text reference].
Our rationale is further discussed in the response to Reviewer #1 Comment #2.

> 2. The manuscript interprets CCC components based on known biology through case studies but does not systematically validate them to demonstrate that the identified programs reflect coherent biological processes.
>    It is unclear whether these components/programs represent distinct biological processes or mathematical artifacts of the decomposition.
>    The authors should perform GO enrichment analysis for the top-weighted L-R pairs associated with each component to support the biological interpretation of the identified communication programs.
>    Particularly for the condition-specific programs, does the enriched biological processes reflect the condition states?
>    In addition, GO enrichment analysis should also be performed for the differentially weighted genes identified by logistic regression, such as those shown in Fig. 4q, r, w, and x.

We agree that biological coherence should be tested rather than argued, and we have added various quantitations to support this.

<!-- Paragraph 1: negative GO results -->
- We attempted to perform gene set enrichment on highly weighted LR pairs for each component in each dataset.
- We observed no significant GO terms in any case.
- We hypothesize why:

<!-- Paragraph 2: coordinated immune programs/LR co-variation analysis -->
- In place of gene set enrichment, to quantify biological coherence, we present a co-variation analysis among top-weighted LR pairs of outcome-associatedd components.
- We present these results in [Figure 3 XXX] and [Figure 5 XXX] and define the process in Methods section [XXX]
- We further bolster the biological coherence of CCC-RISE components using the previously described NicheNet and NICHES validations.
- Together these address the mathematical-artifact concern from two directions---the component's LR pairs move together in expression space and their known gene targets are visibly upregulated in the cells the component says are receiving.

> 3. The authors compute communication scores as the product of ligand and receptor expression between eigen-states.
>    However, this simple calculation does not involve any statistical test and may produce incorrect cell-cell communication inferences between eigen-states as well as between individual cells.
>    The authors should demonstrate whether the inferred communication patterns are robust to alternative CCC score calculation frameworks, such as those used in CellChat and CellPhoneDB.

We agree, and this comment overlaps with Reviewer #1 Comment #6 on statistical robustness of communication tensor entries.
Briefly, we add a cell-permuted null akin to CellChat and CellPhoneDB that generates a null distribution of communication tensor entries with which CCC-RISE communication tensor entries are compared.
Additionally, the reviewer was correct to raise concerns over incorrect CCC scores resulting from the expression product, which is discussed in detail in Reviewer #1 Comment #3.
Briefly, the expression product between two negatively loaded genes resulted in a spurious positive communication score, which we address by adding back per-gene mean expression before computing communication scores.
Please see the referenced reviewer responses for more detailed explanations.

To address the reviewer's third point, we implemented four interchangeable scoring functions and confirmed each behaves as expected on held-out unit tests: our original expression product; the arithmetic-mean score; a geometric-mean variant; and a CellChat-style saturating Hill function.
All three non-product options are defined to require non-negative input and clip accordingly, exactly like CellChat and CellPhoneDB's own formulations, a requirement our re-centering fix now satisfies for RISE eigen-state loadings, and that would otherwise have produced errors (e.g. `NaN`s from a negative-argument square root in the geometric-mean score) or nonsensical output (an unbounded, sometimes-negative "saturating" score) had it been fed the original signed loadings.
We report a comparison between communication programs identified by each of these scoring methods in [figure S_ccc_scoring] and describe the approach in detail in Methods section [XXX].

> 4. Although metrics were provided to guide the selection of the two key hyperparameters (number of RISE components and number of CPD components), it remains unclear why 35 RISE components and 8 CPD components were chosen rather than, for example, 30-50 RISE components or 6-12 CPD components.
>    The metrics do not provide clear guidance for hyperparameter selection.
>    Moreover, the authors evaluated their method on only two datasets but used different metrics to determine the two components (Fig. S1d-g and Fig. 4b-d).
>    This further demonstrates the difficulty of selecting these hyperparameters in practical use.
>    The authors should provide consistent and sharp metrics to allow easy hyperparameter selection.
>    More importantly, a sensitivity analysis should be performed to show how identified components and biological conclusions change across parameter ranges and random seeds of the RISE and CPD factorization.
>    In addition, the authors describe the Factor Match Score in the Methods section to evaluate the stability of the RISE and CPD factorization but do not use it in the data analysis.

We agree, and rank selection has been reworked so that a single criterion applies to both datasets and neither criterion consults sample labels.

The RISE rank is selected by bi-cross-validation: the model is fit with blocks of the expression data held out, and the rank is chosen by reconstruction of those held-out entries.
The CPD rank is selected by collinearity between components of the LR pair mode together with stability of factorizations under re-initialization.
Both criteria are computed by the same runner, with the same parameters, for both datasets, and both depend only on the molecular data.
The multi-replicate nature of these rank selection procedures also serves as a sensitivity analysis under a parameter sweep, where the paramter is rank.
[Add some words on the "sharpness" of each metric. BiCV is sharp for ALAD, not for IBD. CPD criteria are sharp for both.]
The new rank-selection procedure is showcased in [Figure 2 A--D] and described in detail in Methods sections [XXX, YYY].

We now also use the Factor Match Score (FMS) to compare individual fits during sensitivity analyses rather than only defining it.
At the final rank as selected by the above procedures, components are refit under two perturbations---leave-one-patient-out jackknife and re-initializing with a different random seed---and each component is matched to a reference fit by Hungarian assignment and scored by FMS.
Patient jackknife interrogates the contribution of individual patients to the stability of factorization results.
Random-seed refitting serves as the reference point for how much of the observed spread is attributable to the data rather than to initialization.
The results of these sensitivity analyses are reported in [Figure 2 supplementary], [Figure 4 supplementary], and described in detail in Methods section [xxx]

> 5. Different methods were used for identifying condition-specific components across datasets, and inconsistent results were observed.
>    In the COVID-19 analysis, the authors use Spearman correlation between condition factors and disease severity to identify condition-specific components (Components 3, 5, 8).
>    In the ALAD analysis, they use logistic regression (Components 5, 13, 17).
>    This inconsistency undermines comparability and raises questions about the robustness of the findings.
>    Moreover, these condition-specific components are not consistently reflected in the inferred condition factor matrix (e.g., Fig. S5h and Fig. 4d).
>    From the condition factor matrix, almost all components appear highly enriched in the ALAD declined condition.
>    In the COVID-19 analysis, no components were enriched in the Control condition.
>    While quantitative methods such as Spearman correlation and logistic regression are valuable for identifying condition-specific components, the results should be consistent with the fundamental inferred condition factors.

We agree, and the two datasets are now analyzed identically.
The original difference was historical: Spearman correlation was used for the COVID-19 data because the pseudobulk analysis we were comparing against had done so.
In the revision, component--condition associations are tested by ANOVA in both datasets, with multiple-testing correction across components and outcomes (Methods section [XXX]).

On consistency with the condition factors: we now present the association result and the condition loadings together, so the reported association can be read off the factor itself ([Figure 3A]).
The component associated with six-month ALAD outcome shows a monotone, step-wise separation across outcome groups, which is visible in the raw condition factor and is not an artifact of the test.
We would also like to clarify what the condition factor is and is not: because the tensor is centered, components describe *variation* in communication around the cohort average rather than total communication, so a component loading uniformly high in one group reflects the direction of that variation, and the apparent absence of "control-enriched" components in the original figure reflects sign convention and scaling rather than the absence of control-associated signal.
The revised figures state the normalization on the colorbar (see Reviewer #2 Minor Comment #5), which we expect resolves most of this reading.

> 6. The mathematical symbols in the equations and their biological meanings are not consistently defined or clearly explained.
>    The Methods section jumps between concepts without a logical flow, making it difficult to follow.
>    It would be much more helpful to restructure the Methods section to describe the workflow sequentially according to Fig. 1: (1) Reduction and Insight in Single-cell Exploration (RISE) to obtain eigen-states, (2) construction of the aligned 4D communication tensor, and (3) Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD) to extract communication programs.
>    Please clearly define each mathematical symbol and its biological interpretation.
>    The mathematical symbols throughout the Methods section should be consistent.

We have revised the Methods section to describe the workflow sequentially according to Fig. 1: RISE to obtain eigen-states, construction of the aligned 4D communication tensor, and CPD to extract communication programs, each now in its own subsection in that order.

We have also gone through the Methods and standardized notation so that each symbol has one meaning throughout.
Previously, the same letters were reused with different meanings in different places: most notably, $R$ denoted both the rank of a decomposition and receptor expression, and the four factor matrices of the CCC-RISE communication tensor were left unnamed until the Factor Match Score equations, where they collided with letters RISE had already assigned to different quantities (e.g., $C$ meant both "gene factor matrix" for RISE and "condition factor matrix" for CPD).
We now reserve lowercase $r$ for rank throughout, so that $R$ refers unambiguously to receptor expression; RISE retains its existing $A$ (condition), $B$ (cell eigen-state), and $C$ (gene) factor matrices; and the communication tensor's four factor matrices are introduced by name where the tensor itself is defined, using a disjoint set of letters ($D$ condition, $E$ sender eigen-state, $F$ receiver eigen-state, $G$ LR pair) that cannot be confused with RISE's.
In the course of this we also caught and corrected a mislabeling in the original Factor Match Score description, which called the RISE gene factor matrix $B$ rather than $C$.

### Minor Comments

> 1. The authors assume that eigen-states (from PARAFAC2) provide a meaningful basis for computing communication scores.
>    However, the relationship between eigen-state loadings and biological cell states is not fully established.
>    Could a simpler approach-such as canonical correlation analysis (CCA) or other dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., PCA, NMF, VAE)-achieve similar results?
>    What are the advantages of PARAFAC2-derived states in capturing communication-relevant heterogeneity?

This is an interesting point.
In fact, at a high level, a similar approach could indeed be taken using other methods that project single cell RNA-seq data into a lower-dimensional space.
As described in our previous work\ [@pmid:40378843], PARAFAC2 is uniquely suited for multi-condition single-cell analysis because it provides a unique solution for decomposing the data into a low-dimensional representation that captures both cell type heterogeneity and quantitation of the variation across conditions.
By contrast, PCA is rotationally invariant and so it and VAE models will not provide a unique solution to provide a reliable basis for interpretable communication scoring.
CCA provides a unique solution, but cannot be easily broken into a description of the differences between conditions, separated from the single-cell variation.
NMF does provide a unique solution, and it is possible to quantitate the abundance of a pattern within each condition, but non-negativity splits counter-balanced regulatory patterns, such as differentiation programs, into multiple non-negative components.
We have expanded our introduction to the manuscript to include a more detailed comparison of these methods and the relative advantage of PARAFAC2 ([Introduction section?].

In unpublished work, we have a more extensive benchmarking between these alternatives.
In fact, we find that, using the bi-cross-validation strategy described above, that PARAFAC2 consistently outperforms all of these methods in prediction of held-out single cell RNA-seq data, suggesting that it is a better representation of the data.
Furthermore, we have traced the reason for this to (1) PARAFAC2's ability to emit a unique solution with relatively minimal constraints, (2) its ability to express counter-regulatory patterns by avoiding non-negativity constraints, and (3) that most cellular programs are not sparse, and that this is often a forced constraint of the methods used in justifying sparsity.
However, this more mechanistic and detailed discussion will have to remain beyond the scope of this manuscript.

> 2. The analysis spans multiple patient samples and conditions, but it is unclear how batch effects, patient heterogeneity, or technical variation are handled.
>    Do the RISE and CPD projections inherently correct for such effects?

We have added an explicit treatment of this in the Methods.
Instead of re-stating that description here, we point the reviewer to the corresponding Methods section [XXX].
The resampling analysis in Reviewer #2 Comment #4 is also the relevant empirical check here: a component driven by a single sample or batch shows up as a component whose factor match score collapses when that sample is not drawn, and we report per-component stability for exactly this reason.

> 3. How should the LR pairs with negative loadings in each inferred component be interpreted?
>    Why not use a non-negative CPD model for better interpretability?

Please refer to Reviewer #1 Comment #3, where we address these important points.
